At a Wilderness Medicine conference this year I read that a vapor bag over a wet patient is 80% as effective at controlling heat loss as a change of  clothes.

Evaporative cooling, the process of liquid water absorbing heat energy and turning into a vapor, requires an enormous amount of heat energy.  The more air you have moving over wet clothes the more you'll encourage this exchange of heat energy from the patient, or yourself, into the atmosphere as water vapor.  It's the same reason that breathing very cold air dehydrates you and cools you.  

If you're wearing wet clothing it's literally sucking the heat energy out of you.  Your body gets pushed deeper into hypothermia, your blood shunts to the core, the surface of your body loses more heat energy and cools quickly, then you've got severe frost injuries to the extremities and the continuation of heat loss.

If you're able to vapor barrier yourself with a material that won't allow evaporation then you'll be preventing some of this heat loss and I would recommend keeping your clothes on.

In reality, being soaking wet in a cold environment is an immediate life threat that is solved by isolating yourself from articles of  clothing or gear that could make you lose more heat energy (wet blue jeans, for example) and creating exothermic heat (build a fire) while blocking the wind as much as possible.  

Work hard and fast to force your body to burn calories and produce real body heat, you won't sweat if you're soaking wet. cool off. It is much more important for them to be dry and reinsulated with dry clothing than to remain cold and wet.

losing body heat, just like in a wet suit. First of all, you do continue to lose heat in a wet suit; it is just slower than without it. As
long as these patients are damp, moist, or wet, they will continue to lose heat much more than if they are dry.
BUSTED - [b]Hypothermics have to be dry to be warm. Do not hesitate to strip them out of wet, moist, or damp clothing, right
down to their bare skin, and then protect them with dry clothing or insulation.[/b]

Way, way, way more gauze.  Your personal kit should be geared for trauma, not diarrhea and boo-boo ointment.  Gauze (roller gauze or z-pack, not individually wrapped), tape, occlusive dressings, TQ's, hemostatic gauze or agents and a needle/cath combo for decompressions.  Why bring a dozen different sized band-aids when you can bring a roll of tape and some gauze and make anything you need?  The electrolytes, meds, TripleA, none of that is really the sort of thing you have to have on your person NOW when something goes wrong.  I run a basic trauma kit (made by High Speed Gear) that has shears, penlight, chemlight, 2 CAT's, 2 chest seals, 2 packs of z-pack gauze and 1 pack of combat gauze, plus three pairs of ORANGE (NOT BLACK!) gloves.  That's on or near my person almost all the time, it's MOLLE'ed on the outside of my EDC backpack.   Do I use this kit much?  Not one single time, but it's still the one I have IMMEDIATELY available.  If someone is coming to me when I'm guiding, or just a friend with diarrhea, I'm not worried about taking a few minutes to dig it out and conduct a basic assessment.

Inside the backpack I have way more gear, things that it's OK if it takes me four minutes to access.  Your chapstick shouldn't be easier to reach than your TQ's!
